home-energy-audit.h1: Home energy audits in St. John's
home-energy-audit.title: Home energy audits in St. John's: EnerGuide evaluations, costs and rebates
home-energy-audit.description: Book an EnerGuide home energy audit in St. John's: 7 licensed organizations, local prices, Newfoundland and Labrador rebates and what 64% pre-1991 housing means for your upgrade list.
home-energy-audit.lede: 7 NRCan-licensed service organizations deliver EnerGuide home evaluations in St. John's. Here's what one costs, what it tends to find in St. John's houses, and which Newfoundland and Labrador rebates it unlocks.

sections.h2: What an evaluation finds in St. John's homes
sections.html:
Of St. John's's 42,120 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 22% were built before 1961 and 64% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. The typical St. John's house dates from 1971–1980, and an evaluation is how you find out what that means for yours: the blower door measures air leakage, the advisor inspects the attic, walls, basement, windows and heating system, and the report ranks upgrades by what they'd save.

St. John's gets about 4,578 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −12.8°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for St-John's International. That's about 16% more heating demand than the middle of the 70 cities we cover. The more heating a climate needs, the more each fix is worth, which is why the evaluation's ranked list matters more in some cities than others.

In the St. John's area, 58% of households heat mainly with electric baseboards, about 7% with a heat pump, about 7% with a boiler and radiators and about 6% with a forced-air furnace; electricity is the main heating energy for 65% of households and oil for 12% (Statistics Canada, 2023). The heating system on the report shapes the recommendations: a forced-air furnace invites a ducted heat pump, electric baseboards a ductless one.

sections.h2: What it costs in St. John's
sections.html:
There's no province-wide price; takeCHARGE lists the service organizations working in the province without prices.

  • Make the Shift subsidized initial energy audit: For a limited time, Shift Program participants in St. John's can get an initial energy audit (EnerGuide) subsidized to $99, which the City describes as 80% off the regular cost. Book at maketheshiftnl.ca, 709-979-0362 or hello@maketheshiftnl.ca. Details

Most providers quote the initial (pre-upgrade) and follow-up (post-upgrade) visits separately. Rebate programs that pay on measured improvement need both, so ask for the combined price.

sections.h2: How it works
sections.html:
• Initial evaluation, about 2–3 hours. The advisor measures and inspects the house and runs the blower door test.
  • Report and EnerGuide rating. You get the home's energy rating in gigajoules per year and a list of recommended upgrades with estimated savings.
  • Do the work. Most rebate programs only count upgrades done after the initial evaluation.
  • Follow-up evaluation. A second visit measures the improvement, which is what most rebates pay on.

Read the full guide to home energy audits.

blower-door-test.h1: Blower door testing in St. John's
blower-door-test.title: Blower door test in St. John's: cost, who does it and why it matters here
blower-door-test.description: Where to get a blower door test in St. John's, what it costs, and why air leakage matters with 4,578 heating degree-days a year and 22% of houses built before 1961.
blower-door-test.lede: A blower door test measures how leaky a house is and shows where the leaks are. In St. John's, with about 4,578 heating degree-days a year, every leak runs up the heating bill for most of the year.

sections.h2: Why air leakage matters in St. John's
sections.html:
St. John's gets about 4,578 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −12.8°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for St-John's International. That's about 16% more heating demand than the middle of the 70 cities we cover.

Of St. John's's 42,120 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 22% were built before 1961 and 64% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Older houses usually test leakier than newer ones, and an EnerGuide report compares your result with homes of the same era, so you can see whether your house is typical or a problem.

sections.h2: After you seal: two checks
sections.html:
• Combustion safety. In the St. John's area, the main heating energy is oil for 12% of households. A tighter house changes how fuel-burning appliances vent, so the spillage check should be repeated after serious air sealing. Combustion safety testing in St. John's
  • Radon. Sealing shifts the pressure balance between the house and the soil. Health Canada's 2012 survey found 4% of 100 homes tested in the Eastern Regional Integrated Health Authority health region above the guideline. In the City of St. John's free test-kit program, about 345 kits went out in November 2024 and 278 homes completed testing over the winter; about one in ten of them were above Health Canada's 200 Bq/m³ guideline. The participants were volunteers, so it isn't a random survey. Test before and after big air-sealing jobs. Radon testing in St. John's

sections.h2: What it costs in St. John's
sections.html: A blower door test is part of every EnerGuide evaluation rather than a separate purchase. There's no province-wide price; takeCHARGE lists the service organizations working in the province without prices.

sections.h2: How the test works
sections.html:
• A calibrated fan is fitted into an exterior door and pulls air out until the house is at 50 pascals, the standard test pressure.
  • The result is air changes per hour at 50 Pa (ACH50): how many times an hour the whole volume of air would leak out and be replaced at that pressure.
  • While the fan runs, you and the advisor walk the house and feel for leaks at the attic hatch, rim joists, pot lights, trim and plumbing and wiring penetrations.
  • A second test after the work shows what changed, and it is what most rebates pay on.

The blower door test in detail.

faq.q: How much does a blower door test cost in St. John's?

faq.q: What is a good blower door result?

thermal-imaging.title: Thermal imaging home inspection in St. John's: when to book and who does it
thermal-imaging.description: Infrared (thermal) home inspections in St. John's: when St. John's's weather gives a clear scan, what the camera finds in local houses, and the licensed advisors who bring one.
thermal-imaging.lede: An infrared camera shows missing insulation, air leaks and damp spots without opening a wall, but only when it's at least 10°C colder outside than inside. St. John's's long heating season gives you months of good scanning weather.

sections.h2: When to book in St. John's
sections.html: St. John's gets about 4,578 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −12.8°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for St-John's International. That gives St. John's a long window, roughly late fall to early spring, when the inside-outside difference comfortably exceeds the 10°C an infrared scan needs.

sections.h2: What the camera finds in St. John's houses
sections.html: Of St. John's's 42,120 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 22% were built before 1961 and 64% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Older houses are where the camera earns its keep: empty or settled wall cavities, gaps at the top of walls, and cold corners where framing bridges the insulation. Run it with the blower door test depressurizing the house and every leak shows up as a cold streak.

sections.h2: What it costs
sections.html: Most EnerGuide advisors include an infrared scan with the evaluation, but it isn't required, so confirm when you book. There's no province-wide price; takeCHARGE lists the service organizations working in the province without prices.

faq.q: When is the best time for a thermal imaging inspection in St. John's?
faq.a: Late fall through early spring, when it is at least 10°C colder outside than inside. Cold, overcast days with no direct sun on the walls give the clearest images.

faq.q: Can a thermal camera see through walls?
faq.a: No. It reads surface temperatures. Missing insulation or an air leak shows up because it changes the temperature of the wall or ceiling surface.

heat-loss-calculation.h1: Heat loss calculations in St. John's
heat-loss-calculation.title: Heat loss calculation in St. John's: sizing a heat pump for −12.8°C
heat-loss-calculation.description: A CSA F280 room-by-room heat loss calculation for St. John's homes, sized to the local −12.8°C design temperature: why it matters for heat pumps, what it costs and who does it.
heat-loss-calculation.lede: The heat loss calculation is how a heat pump or furnace gets sized for your house, and the key input is the design temperature: −12.8°C for St. John's, from NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for St-John's International.

sections.h2: Why the design temperature matters in St. John's
sections.html:
−12.8°C is the 12th-mildest design temperature of the 70 cities we cover. The F280 calculation works out how much heat each room loses on that design day, from the house's actual walls, windows, air leakage and ceiling insulation.

At −12.8°C, a cold-climate heat pump sized to the calculation can carry most of the season, and the number shows how much backup heat the coldest days need.

In the St. John's area, 58% of households heat mainly with electric baseboards, about 7% with a heat pump, about 7% with a boiler and radiators and about 6% with a forced-air furnace; electricity is the main heating energy for 65% of households and oil for 12% (Statistics Canada, 2023).

sections.h2: Why skipping it costs money
sections.html: Contractors who size by square footage routinely oversize. An oversized heat pump costs more to buy, cycles on and off, dehumidifies poorly in summer and wears faster. An undersized one leans on backup heat. The F280 report is the evidence either way, and it's worth having before you compare quotes.

sections.h2: What it costs
sections.html: About $150–$400 as a standalone calculation (a September 2026 planning range; quotes vary). Many energy advisors bundle it with an EnerGuide evaluation, which also gives the calculation measured air-leakage data instead of an assumption.

providers.note: Many energy advisors also do room-by-room CSA F280 calculations for an extra fee; HVAC designers do them too. Ask for the F280 report itself, not just an equipment recommendation.

duct-leakage-testing.h1: Duct leakage testing in St. John's
duct-leakage-testing.title: Duct leakage testing in St. John's: cold rooms, costs and who tests
duct-leakage-testing.description: Duct leakage and airflow testing in St. John's: about 6% of local households heat with a forced-air furnace, why far rooms stay cold, what a test costs and who does it.
duct-leakage-testing.lede: If some rooms never get warm, the problem is often the ductwork, not the furnace. In the St. John's area, only about 6% of households heat with a forced-air furnace, so the test matters mainly for homes with ducts or those adding a ducted heat pump.

sections.h2: Who needs it in St. John's
sections.html:
In the St. John's area, 58% of households heat mainly with electric baseboards, about 7% with a heat pump, about 7% with a boiler and radiators and about 6% with a forced-air furnace; electricity is the main heating energy for 65% of households and oil for 12% (Statistics Canada, 2023).

Electric baseboards outnumber furnaces here, and a baseboard-heated house has no ducts to test. The test matters if you have forced air, or before you add a ducted heat pump to existing ductwork.

Of St. John's's 42,120 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 22% were built before 1961 and 64% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Ducts in older houses often run through unheated spaces with taped or unsealed joints, and supply runs to the far rooms are the first to suffer.

sections.h2: What the test shows
sections.html:
• Total duct leakage, as a share of the system's airflow, measured with a duct-pressurization fan.
  • Airflow at each register, which explains why one bedroom is always cold.
  • Whether sealing and balancing will fix comfort problems before you buy bigger equipment.

Duct leakage testing in detail.

sections.h2: What it costs
sections.html: About $200–$450 (a September 2026 planning range; quotes vary). It isn't part of a standard EnerGuide evaluation, so ask for it when you book if comfort is your main complaint.

combustion-safety-test.h1: Combustion safety testing in St. John's
combustion-safety-test.title: Combustion safety testing in St. John's: spillage checks before you seal
combustion-safety-test.description: Combustion spillage and venting checks for St. John's homes with gas, oil or wood appliances, and why they matter before air sealing.
combustion-safety-test.lede: A combustion safety test checks that your furnace, water heater and fireplace vent their exhaust outside instead of into the house, which matters most right before and after you tighten the house up. In the St. John's area, the main heating energy is oil for 12% of households.

sections.h2: Why it matters in St. John's
sections.html:
In the St. John's area, 58% of households heat mainly with electric baseboards, about 7% with a heat pump, about 7% with a boiler and radiators and about 6% with a forced-air furnace; electricity is the main heating energy for 65% of households and oil for 12% (Statistics Canada, 2023).

St. John's has no piped natural gas for homes, so combustion appliances here are mostly oil, propane or wood, and each needs its own venting check.

The risk rises after air sealing: a tighter house plus a strong exhaust fan or dryer can pull exhaust back down a chimney. That's why advisors test for spillage during an evaluation and why it should be repeated after serious tightening.

sections.h2: The CO alarm rule in Newfoundland and Labrador
sections.html: Newfoundland and Labrador's fire regulations require smoke alarms in existing homes but contain no CO alarm requirement.

sections.h2: What the check involves
sections.html:
• Worst-case depressurization: exhaust fans and the dryer on, doors set to make the appliance room as negative as it gets.
  • A spillage and draft check at each appliance, with a CO reading.
  • A plan if anything fails: often a sealed-combustion appliance or a fix to the venting, done by a licensed gas or oil technician.

The combustion safety check in detail.

faq.a: Newfoundland and Labrador's fire regulations require smoke alarms in existing homes but contain no CO alarm requirement.

faq.q: I have CO alarms. Isn't that enough?

ventilation-assessment.h1: Ventilation and humidity assessments in St. John's
ventilation-assessment.title: Ventilation and humidity assessment in St. John's: condensation, mold and HRVs
ventilation-assessment.description: Why St. John's homes get window condensation and musty air, what a ventilation and humidity assessment measures, and when an HRV or ERV makes sense. 26% of local houses were built since 2001.
ventilation-assessment.lede: Condensation on windows, musty basements and stuffy bedrooms are ventilation and humidity problems, and they're easy to confuse with insulation problems. A ventilation assessment measures which one you have.

sections.h2: Why St. John's homes get humidity problems
sections.html:
St. John's gets about 4,578 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −12.8°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for St-John's International. On St. John's's coldest days, window glass and poorly insulated corners get cold enough for condensation at humidity levels that feel normal indoors, so winter humidity needs to stay at the lower end of the comfortable range.

Of St. John's's 42,120 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 22% were built before 1961 and 64% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Newer houses (26% of St. John's's were built since 2001) are tight and usually have an HRV or ERV that needs balancing and cleaning. Older houses that get air-sealed can lose the accidental ventilation they used to rely on.

sections.h2: What the assessment measures
sections.html:
• Relative humidity in living areas and the basement.
  • Actual airflow from bath and kitchen fans, and whether they vent outside rather than into the attic.
  • How much fresh air the house gets, and whether an HRV or ERV is balanced.

The ventilation and humidity assessment in detail.

faq.q: HRV or ERV?
faq.a: Both bring in fresh air and recover heat. An ERV also transfers some moisture, which helps keep very dry winter air from getting drier; an HRV suits houses that tend to run humid.

faq.q: Why did condensation appear after we got new windows?
faq.a: Tighter windows cut accidental air leakage, so humidity builds up. The fix is usually controlled ventilation, not leakier windows.

attic-insulation-inspection.h1: Attic insulation inspections in St. John's
attic-insulation-inspection.title: Attic insulation inspection in St. John's: depth, air leaks and vermiculite
attic-insulation-inspection.description: What an attic inspection finds in St. John's houses (64% built before 1991), why insulation pays with 4,578 heating degree-days, and the rebates for topping it up.
attic-insulation-inspection.lede: The attic is usually the cheapest big energy fix in a house, and the inspection decides how to do it: how much insulation is there, where air leaks through the ceiling, and whether anything up there must not be disturbed.

sections.h2: What inspections find in St. John's attics
sections.html:
Of St. John's's 42,120 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 22% were built before 1961 and 64% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Attics in older houses commonly have a fraction of today's recommended insulation, and top-ups done over the years often buried air leaks instead of sealing them first.

St. John's gets about 4,578 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −12.8°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for St-John's International. That's about 16% more heating demand than the middle of the 70 cities we cover. The colder the climate, the faster added attic insulation pays for itself.

Vermiculite. Loose, pebbly, grey-brown or silver-gold insulation may contain asbestos. Health Canada's advice is not to disturb it; have it sampled before any attic work. Asbestos and vermiculite testing in St. John's

sections.h2: The right order for the work
sections.html:
• Seal the air leaks first: top plates, pot lights, plumbing stacks, the hatch.
  • Fix ventilation baffles so new insulation doesn't block soffit vents.
  • Then top up the insulation. Burying unsealed leaks under new insulation wastes much of the benefit.

What an attic inspection checks.

radon-testing.title: Radon testing in St. John's: local levels, test kits and certified professionals
radon-testing.description: Radon in St. John's: Health Canada survey results for the Eastern Regional Integrated Health Authority region (4% above the guideline), how to test for 3+ months, where to get kits and C-NRPP professionals locally.
radon-testing.lede: Radon is invisible, has no smell, and is the second-leading cause of lung cancer in Canada. In Health Canada's national survey, 4% of homes tested in the Eastern Regional Integrated Health Authority health region were above the guideline, and the only way to know about your house is to test it.

sections.h2: Radon in St. John's
sections.html:
Health Canada's 2012 survey found 4% of 100 homes tested in the Eastern Regional Integrated Health Authority health region above the guideline. In the City of St. John's free test-kit program, about 345 kits went out in November 2024 and 278 homes completed testing over the winter; about one in ten of them were above Health Canada's 200 Bq/m³ guideline. The participants were volunteers, so it isn't a random survey.

No survey can tell you about a single house, because neighbouring homes can differ widely. Testing is the only way to know.

sections.h2: How to test properly
sections.html:
• Use a long-term test of at least three months, with most of it in the heating season, which gives the most conservative result.
  • Place the detector in the lowest level you spend four or more hours a day in, away from drafts, and follow the kit's instructions.
  • If the result is above 200 Bq/m³, Health Canada recommends fixing it within a year, sooner if it's much higher.

Our full radon testing guide.

sections.h2: Kits and professionals in St. John's
sections.html:
• There's no provincial kit program; several NL public libraries lend radon monitors.
  • The City of St. John's has run free radon kit programs for residents, including about 250 kits in its November 2025 round.
  • For a professional measurement or mitigation, search the C-NRPP directory by your St. John's postal code; it lists certified measurement and mitigation professionals.

sections.h2: Rules and help in Newfoundland and Labrador
sections.html:
• Newfoundland and Labrador leaves building rules for new houses to municipal by-laws, so radon measures in new homes depend on the municipality.
  • The Canadian Lung Association's Lungs Matter program offers up to $1,500 toward mitigation for households with low to moderate incomes or a lung cancer diagnosis.
  • If your level is high, mitigation (usually a sub-slab depressurization fan system installed by a C-NRPP-certified professional) typically costs $2,000–$4,000.

faq.q: Is radon a problem in St. John's?
faq.a: Health Canada's 2012 survey found 4% of 100 homes tested in the Eastern Regional Integrated Health Authority health region above the guideline. In the City of St. John's free test-kit program, about 345 kits went out in November 2024 and 278 homes completed testing over the winter; about one in ten of them were above Health Canada's 200 Bq/m³ guideline. The participants were volunteers, so it isn't a random survey. Any home can have high radon, so Health Canada recommends testing every home.

faq.q: How long should a radon test take?
faq.a: At least three months, with most of it during the heating season. Short tests can't tell you your long-term average.

faq.q: Where can I get a radon test kit in St. John's?
faq.a: There's no provincial kit program; several NL public libraries lend radon monitors. Hardware stores and lung associations also sell long-term kits for about $30–$60.

faq.q: What does radon mitigation cost?
faq.a: Typically $2,000–$4,000 for a sub-slab depressurization system installed by a C-NRPP-certified professional.

carbon-monoxide-testing.h1: Carbon monoxide testing in St. John's
carbon-monoxide-testing.title: Carbon monoxide testing in St. John's: the Newfoundland and Labrador alarm rules and appliance checks
carbon-monoxide-testing.description: CO safety for St. John's homes: what Newfoundland and Labrador law requires, where alarms go and how appliances get checked.
carbon-monoxide-testing.lede: Carbon monoxide is odourless and can kill. Newfoundland and Labrador's fire regulations require smoke alarms in existing homes but contain no CO alarm requirement.

sections.h2: The rule in Newfoundland and Labrador
sections.html: Newfoundland and Labrador's fire regulations require smoke alarms in existing homes but contain no CO alarm requirement.

sections.h2: CO sources in St. John's homes
sections.html:
In the St. John's area, the main heating energy is oil for 12% of households (Statistics Canada, 2023). Any fuel-burning appliance, fireplace or attached garage is a potential CO source.

There's no piped natural gas for homes in St. John's, so the usual CO sources are oil furnaces, propane appliances, wood stoves and attached garages.

Single-detached houses make up 42% of St. John's's households; many have an attached garage, another reason to put an alarm near the door into the house.

sections.h2: What a CO check involves
sections.html:
• Alarms next to sleeping areas and on every storey, tested monthly and replaced by their end-of-life date (usually 7 to 10 years).
  • Annual service of fuel-burning appliances by a licensed technician.
  • A combustion spillage test during an energy evaluation, which catches a venting problem before it produces CO.

Our carbon monoxide guide · Combustion safety testing in St. John's

faq.q: Are carbon monoxide alarms mandatory in St. John's?
faq.a: Newfoundland and Labrador's fire regulations require smoke alarms in existing homes but contain no CO alarm requirement.

faq.q: Where should CO alarms go?
faq.a: Outside every sleeping area and on every storey, following the manufacturer's instructions. Some rules also call for one near a fuel-burning appliance or the door from an attached garage.

faq.q: How long do CO alarms last?
faq.a: Most have an end-of-life date of 7 to 10 years printed on the unit; replace them by then even if they still beep when tested.

mold-testing.h1: Mold and air quality testing in St. John's
mold-testing.title: Mold testing in St. John's: air quality sampling and finding the moisture source
mold-testing.description: Mold and indoor air quality testing in St. John's: when sampling is worth $300–$600, why damp coastal winters cause condensation, and how to find an accredited lab.
mold-testing.lede: Mold sampling tells you whether there's a hidden mold problem and roughly where. It doesn't tell you why, and fixing the moisture source is the actual cure.

sections.h2: Why mold shows up in St. John's homes
sections.html:
St. John's gets about 4,578 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −12.8°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for St-John's International. Mild, wet winters keep materials damp, so poorly vented bathrooms, basements and crawlspaces are the usual suspects.

Of St. John's's 42,120 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 22% were built before 1961 and 64% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Older basements without a moisture barrier and houses that were air-sealed without adding ventilation are common trouble spots.

sections.h2: When sampling is worth it
sections.html:
• You smell mustiness but can't find the source.
  • After a leak or flood, to check that cleanup worked.
  • Before buying an older house with signs of past water damage.

If you can see mould, you usually don't need a test to know it's there; you need to fix the moisture and clean it up properly.

No Canadian province has a mandatory mould standard for homes. Health Canada's guideline sets no numerical limit: it says to fix moisture problems and clean up visible mould.

sections.h2: Choosing a tester and lab
sections.html:
Ask any St. John's tester which lab analyzes their samples, and look for one accredited under AIHA's EMLAP program for environmental microbiology. Pair sampling with a ventilation and humidity assessment, which finds the cause.

Ventilation and humidity assessments in St. John's · Our mold and indoor air quality guide

faq.q: How much does mold testing cost in St. John's?
faq.a: Plan on about $300–$600 for a typical sampling visit (a September 2026 planning range); lab fees for extra samples add to that.

faq.q: Do I need a test if I can see mould?
faq.a: Usually not. Visible mould needs cleanup and a fix for the moisture source. Testing helps most when you suspect mould you can't see.

faq.q: Is there a legal mould limit for homes in Canada?
faq.a: No. Health Canada sets no numerical limit; its guidance is to control moisture and clean up mould. Quebec has a voluntary handling standard.

asbestos-testing.h1: Asbestos and vermiculite testing in St. John's
asbestos-testing.title: Asbestos testing in St. John's: vermiculite, labs and the Newfoundland and Labrador rules
asbestos-testing.description: Asbestos and vermiculite testing in St. John's, where 64% of houses were built before 1991: what to sample, lab costs and the Newfoundland and Labrador rules for renovation.
asbestos-testing.lede: About 26,700 St. John's houses (64%) were built before 1991, when asbestos still turned up in insulation, flooring, plaster and duct wrap. A lab test before renovation is the only way to know.

sections.h2: Where asbestos shows up in St. John's houses
sections.html:
Of St. John's's 42,120 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 22% were built before 1961 and 64% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census.

  • Vermiculite attic insulation: loose, pebbly, grey-brown or silver-gold granules.
  • Vinyl floor tiles and their adhesive, textured ceilings and some plaster.
  • Duct wrap and pipe insulation on older heating systems.

sections.h2: The rules in Newfoundland and Labrador
sections.html:
In Newfoundland and Labrador, only certified asbestos abatement contractors may remove asbestos, and removal needs written notice to the OHS Division and a disposal permit.

Whatever the rules, don't sand, cut or remove suspect material yourself before it's tested.

sections.h2: Testing and labs
sections.html:
A trained assessor takes small samples, and an accredited lab analyzes them; plan on about $50–$150 per sample. Asbestos labs in Canada are typically accredited under NIST's NVLAP program.

Our asbestos and vermiculite guide · Attic inspections in St. John's

faq.q: Do I need an asbestos test before renovating in St. John's?
faq.a: If the house was built before 1991 and the work will disturb insulation, flooring, plaster or duct wrap, test first. In Newfoundland and Labrador, only certified asbestos abatement contractors may remove asbestos, and removal needs written notice to the OHS Division and a disposal permit.

faq.q: How much does asbestos testing cost?
faq.a: About $50–$150 per lab sample, plus the assessor's visit. Abatement, if needed, is quoted separately.

faq.q: What should I do if I have vermiculite in the attic?
faq.a: Leave it alone, keep the attic closed, and have it sampled before any attic work. Health Canada advises against disturbing it or removing it yourself.

lead-paint-testing.h1: Lead paint testing in St. John's
lead-paint-testing.title: Lead paint testing in St. John's: which homes are at risk and how to test
lead-paint-testing.description: 22% of St. John's's houses were built before 1961, when lead paint was common. How to test with $15–$40 swabs or a lab, and how to renovate safely.
lead-paint-testing.lede: Health Canada says a home built before 1960 probably has lead paint somewhere. That's 22% of St. John's's houses (built before 1961, per the 2021 Census), plus exterior paint on many of the 42% built from 1961 to 1990.

sections.h2: Which St. John's homes are at risk
sections.html:
Of St. John's's 42,120 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 22% were built before 1961 and 64% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census.

  • Built before 1960: probably has lead-based paint (Health Canada).
  • Built 1960–1990: exterior paint may contain lead, and interior paint may contain smaller amounts.
  • Built after 1990: consumer paints were virtually lead-free by then.

sections.h2: How to test
sections.html:
• Swab kits ($15–$40) give a quick screen of the surfaces you plan to disturb.
  • For certainty, send paint chips to a lab accredited under AIHA's ELLAP program, or hire a firm with an X-ray fluorescence (XRF) analyzer.
  • Test before sanding, stripping or replacing old windows and trim.

Our lead paint guide.

sections.h2: If it's positive
sections.html: Don't dry-sand, use a heat gun or power-wash it. Contain the work area, mist surfaces, clean with a HEPA vacuum, and keep children and pregnant people away until cleanup is done. No province has a lead-paint rule aimed at homeowners, but contractors in B.C. and Yukon must include lead in pre-renovation or demolition hazard inspections.

faq.q: Does my St. John's house have lead paint?
faq.a: If it was built before 1960, probably; 1960–1990, possibly on the exterior. Test the surfaces you plan to disturb.

faq.q: Are lead test swabs reliable?
faq.a: They are a useful screen. For renovation decisions, confirm with a lab analysis of paint chips or an XRF reading.

faq.q: What does lead paint testing cost?
faq.a: Swab kits run about $15–$40; lab analysis and XRF testing cost more and are quoted by the firm.

well-water-testing.h1: Well water testing in St. John's
well-water-testing.title: Well water testing in St. John's: how to test and what it costs in Newfoundland and Labrador
well-water-testing.description: Private well water testing in St. John's: some rural areas rely on private wells. How Newfoundland and Labrador's testing program works, what it costs and how often to test.
well-water-testing.lede: Most of St. John's is on municipal water, but the city's boundaries include rural fringe areas. If yours is, here's how testing works in Newfoundland and Labrador.

sections.h2: Wells in St. John's
sections.html:
Most of St. John's is on municipal water, but the city's boundaries include rural fringe areas.

Local program: For the free provincial bacteria test, St. John's samples go to the NL Public Health Laboratory at the Miller Centre rather than a Government Service Centre. Details

sections.h2: How testing works in Newfoundland and Labrador
sections.html: Free bacteria testing: sterile bottles are at Government Service Centres and the NL Public Health Laboratory. Chemistry goes to an approved private lab for a fee.

sections.h2: What to test for
sections.html:
• Bacteria (total coliforms and E. coli): at least once a year, and after flooding, heavy rain or work on the well.
  • Nitrate, especially near farmland or septic systems.
  • Metals and naturally occurring contaminants such as arsenic, uranium or manganese when a well is new and every few years after, depending on local geology.

Our well water guide.

faq.q: Is well water testing free in Newfoundland and Labrador?
faq.a: Free bacteria testing: sterile bottles are at Government Service Centres and the NL Public Health Laboratory. Chemistry goes to an approved private lab for a fee.

faq.q: How often should I test my well?
faq.a: For bacteria, at least once a year and after flooding, heavy rain or well work; many health units recommend more often. Test chemistry when the well is new and every few years after.

faq.q: Are private wells common in St. John's?
faq.a: Most of St. John's is on municipal water, but the city's boundaries include rural fringe areas.

commercial-energy-audit.h1: Commercial energy audits in St. John's
commercial-energy-audit.title: Commercial energy audits in St. John's: reporting rules and incentives
commercial-energy-audit.description: Commercial and multi-unit building energy audits in St. John's: ASHRAE levels, no mandatory reporting rule, and 1 utility or government incentive for audits and studies.
commercial-energy-audit.lede: Offices, apartment buildings, retail and industrial sites get engineering energy audits rather than EnerGuide evaluations. Here's what applies in St. John's: no mandatory reporting rule and 1 incentive program we found for audits and studies.

sections.h2: Reporting rules that apply in St. John's
sections.html: • No city-specific rule found (none found): No municipal energy/water benchmarking, reporting or building-performance by-law found; provincial rules apply (see rules.provinces.NL).

sections.h2: Incentives for audits and studies
sections.html: • Business Efficiency Program - Custom Solutions (takeCHARGE (Newfoundland Power and Newfoundland and Labrador Hydro)): Step 1 is a high-level energy assessment by a TakeCharge energy expert, 'fully funded by TakeCharge'; where a detailed energy audit or feasibility study is needed, 'TakeCharge funding may also be available' (no amount stated). Upgrade incentive: $0.10/kWh of first-year savings, max $100,000, plus a limited-time bonus of $500 per kW of peak demand reduced (offer until Dec 31, 2026; measures in service by Dec 31, 2027). Details

sections.h2: Audit levels
sections.html:
• Level 1, walk-through: a site visit and bill review that benchmarks the building and lists low-cost measures.
  • Level 2, energy survey and analysis: where the energy goes, with savings and cost estimates per measure. Most incentive applications use this level.
  • Level 3, detailed analysis: monitoring and modelling for capital-intensive projects.

Ask which level a quote covers. Audits are done by engineering firms and energy consultants; look for a P.Eng. and credentials such as the Certified Energy Manager (CEM). How commercial energy audits work.

faq.q: Do St. John's buildings have to report energy use?
faq.a: We found no mandatory reporting rule for St. John's buildings as of September 28, 2026.

faq.q: Are there incentives for commercial energy audits in St. John's?
faq.a: Yes: Business Efficiency Program - Custom Solutions. Check eligibility and pre-approval rules before you commission the audit.

faq.q: What does a commercial energy audit cost?
faq.a: It depends on the building's size and the ASHRAE level. Get quotes that state the level and the deliverables.
